To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) weed control method (herbicides vs. cultural) did not affect crop yield, but weed species presence and abundance did vary with weed control method; 2) crop yield was affected by fertilizer input, but weed presence and abundance did not vary with fertilizer input; 3) crop yield was not affected by weed control method and fertilizer input in a consistent manner across sites.
weed growth and cereal grain yields could be reduced with reduced herbicide and fertilization inputs, but the impacts were short term and not consistent among sites.
weed species and grain yield of cereal crops in an annual cropping sequence are not impacted by reduced herbicide and N and P fertilizer inputs in the short-term.
In summary, our research is concerned with
reducing the amount of herbicides and fertilizer applied to cereal crops and the impact of such reductions on crop yield and weed growth.
the influence of herbicide and fertilizer use on cereal crop yields and weed growth.
the influence of herbicides and fertilizer on crop yield and weed growth in an annual cropping sequence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
weed species composition and cereal grain yield were not affected by weed control method, whereas cereal grain yield was affected by fertilizer application method.
herbicides can be reduced without yield loss in a cereal crop rotation.
the use of reduced herbicide inputs with cultural weed control is not detrimental to the crop and can be used in the short term without a yield penalty in the Northern Great Plain region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of herbicides is not always needed for the control of all weed species, especially in a cropping system that has a history of good weed control.
the use of reduced herbicide inputs in a cereal grain cropping system can be done with no loss in yield, and in some cases, an increase in grain yield.
weed control with herbicides and fertilizer N and P are important inputs for maximizing cereal crop production.
The main takeaway from our work is that
weed control method (herbicides vs. cultural methods) had no impact on cereal grain yield.
the short-term impact of herbicide inputs is not well understood and may be less important than previously thought in the Northern Great Plain.
weed control method (i.e., herbicides vs. cultural) did not influence cereal grain yield, but fertilizer inputs did influence cereal grain yield and the presence of weed species.
